# Installation

didgpu installs from CRAN in one line. Most users will not need to do anything
beyond that. If you want the latest development commit, or if you have an NVIDIA
GPU and want the CUDA-accelerated backend, keep reading.

## Which install path to use

| Situation | Install path |
| --------- | ------------ |
| You want to use the package | `install.packages("didgpu")` (CRAN) |
| You want features not yet on CRAN | r-universe (below) |
| You have an NVIDIA GPU and plan to run large cluster bootstraps | Source install with CUDA (below) |

The CPU backend powers all the estimators in this book and passes all tests. The
GPU backend is a performance optimization for one particular estimator: large
cluster bootstraps, where it can be 100-200x faster than the pure-R path. For
point estimates and smaller panels, the two are usually within a few percent of
each other. Install CUDA only if you are going to benefit from it.

## Prerequisites

Before installing didgpu, make sure you have:

- R 4.1 or newer. Check that you have it by running `R --version` in a terminal
  or `R.version.string` in R. If you do not have it, download it from
  <https://cran.r-project.org>.
- A working C++ compiler for the Rcpp backend.
- macOS: install the command line tools with `xcode-select --install` in
  Terminal.
- Linux: `build-essential` on Debian/Ubuntu or the Development Tools group on
  Fedora/RHEL.
- Windows: install Rtools45 from <https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/>.
  You need Rtools only when installing from source.
- Optional for the GPU backend: NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit 12.0 or newer with cuBLAS
  and cuSOLVER.
- Optional for the GPU backend: a CUDA-capable GPU with `sm_75` or higher
  compute capability (see below).

The CUDA Toolkit can be downloaded from
<https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads>.

## From CRAN (recommended)

```r
install.packages("didgpu")
```

This installs the pure-R and Rcpp backends, which power all the estimators in
this book. This is all you need to run didgpu.

## From r-universe (development version)

If you want the latest commit on `main` before it is released on CRAN:

```r
install.packages(
  "didgpu",
  repos = c("https://joshuaammons.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org")
)
```

r-universe offers binary packages for macOS, Windows, and Linux, so you get the
latest features without having to build from source.

## From source with GPU support

If you have an NVIDIA GPU and the CUDA Toolkit installed, the source install
compiles the CUDA kernels.

What to expect on a Mac without CUDA. When I installed didgpu on my M1
MacBook, the configure script printed `CUDA toolkit not found. Building CPU-only.` right in the middle of the compiler output, and I thought the install had failed. It had not. On any Mac (and on any machine without an NVIDIA GPU), that message is the expected path: the package builds the CPU backends and skips the GPU one, and the install finishes cleanly a few seconds later with `* DONE (didgpu)`. If you see the CUDA-not-found line and no `ERROR` after it, you are fine.

Step 1. Tell R where to find your CUDA installation:

```r
# Linux
Sys.setenv(CUDA_HOME = "/usr/local/cuda")

# Windows
Sys.setenv(CUDA_PATH = "C:/Program Files/NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit/CUDA/v13.2")
```

Step 2. Install from source:

```r
# From CRAN source
install.packages("didgpu", type = "source")

# Or from GitHub head
remotes::install_github("JoshuaAmmons/didgpu")
```

didgpu's configure script emits a one-line status message at install time,
telling you whether CUDA was found:

```text
didgpu configure
CUDA toolkit detected: /usr/local/cuda
-> Building WITH GPU support.
backends available after install: 'r', 'cpu', 'cuda'
```

If CUDA is not found, the installation proceeds, but only the `r` and `cpu`
backends are built. There is no error, warning, or message. If
`backend = "cuda"` is called later, it will return an informative error.

## Verify your install

No matter how you installed didgpu, verify that it works:

```r
library(didgpu)
packageVersion("didgpu")
#> [1] '0.1.2'
```

If these two lines run without errors, the pure-R and Rcpp backends are
installed.

To check whether the GPU backend is available:

```r
didgpu_has_cuda_support()
#> [1] TRUE
```

A `TRUE` value means that you can pass `backend = "cuda"` to any estimator in
didgpu. If you get `FALSE`, it means that either your system does not have CUDA
installed or didgpu was not built with CUDA support.

## Supported GPUs

didgpu supports GPUs with CUDA compute capabilities from `sm_75` to `sm_120`:

| Architecture | Compute capability | Example cards |
| ------------ | ----------------- | ------------- |
| Turing | `sm_75` | RTX 20-series, T4, GTX 16-series |
| Ampere (data center) | `sm_80` | A100 |
| Ampere (desktop) | `sm_86` | RTX 30-series |
| Ada Lovelace | `sm_89` | RTX 40-series, RTX 4000 |
| Hopper | `sm_90` | H100 |
| Blackwell | `sm_120` | RTX PRO Blackwell, RTX 50-series |

A `compute_120` PTX target is included so that newer Blackwell-and-beyond cards
can JIT-compile the PTX directly.

## System requirements

- R ≥ 4.1
- On Linux and macOS: GNU make (already present on most systems)
- Windows: Rtools45, only when building from source
- Optional for GPU: NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit ≥ 12.0 with cuBLAS, cuSOLVER, cuRAND

## Dependencies

didgpu has a small set of suggested and imported packages: `data.table`,
`Rcpp`, `RcppEigen`, `MASS`, `sandwich`, and `jsonlite`.

The reference packages that didgpu benchmarks against are listed in Suggests, not
Imports: `did`, `DIDmultiplegtDYN`, `DIDmultiplegt`, `fect`, `HonestDiD`, and
`DRDID`. They are only loaded when `backend = "reference"` is used (for
bit-for-bit reproducibility in testing). If you want to run benchmarks, install
the suggested packages:

```r
install.packages(c("did", "DIDmultiplegtDYN", "fect", "HonestDiD"))
```
## Common install failures

- macOS: `xcrun: error: invalid active developer path`. Xcode command line tools
  are missing. Install them by running `xcode-select --install` in Terminal and
  try again.
- macOS: `ld: unsupported tapi file type`. You have newer Command Line Tools
  installed than R was built with. Upgrade R to the latest version from
  https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/.
- macOS: architecture mismatch. If you have an M1, M2, M3, or M4, the arm64
  version of R is recommended. Check by running `Sys.info()[["machine"]]` in
  R. If it returns `"x86_64"`, it means you have the wrong version of R
  installed. Uninstall and reinstall the arm64 version.
- Windows: `make: command not found` or Rtools errors. Rtools is not installed or
  not on your PATH. Download and install Rtools45 from
  https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/.
- Any OS: `configure: error: CUDA toolkit not found` when you intended to build
  with CUDA support. The configure script could not find `nvcc`. Set
  `CUDA_HOME` on Linux/macOS or `CUDA_PATH` on Windows to the root directory of
  the CUDA installation and try again.

## Reporting an install problem

If you have an installation problem that is not listed above, please file an issue at https://github.com/JoshuaAmmons/didgpu/issues with the following information:

- The output of `sessionInfo()` in R
- The output of `Sys.getenv(c("CUDA_HOME", "CUDA_PATH"))`
- The log file from the installation, particularly the lines printed after `install.packages(...)` failed. The lines starting with `didgpu: configure:` are especially useful if you are trying to install the GPU backend.
